Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)


Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
We will show that the minimum is \(\boxed{499}\).

---

## 1. Structural consequences of the condition

From the condition with \(i=j\), we get

\[
|A_i|=i.
\]

If \(a\mid b\), then

\[
|A_a\cap A_b|=\gcd(a,b)=a=|A_a|,
\]

so \(A_a\subseteq A_b\). Hence for any \(i,j\), letting \(g=\gcd(i,j)\),

\[
A_g\subseteq A_i\cap A_j
\]

and both sets have size \(g\), so

\[
A_i\cap A_j=A_{\gcd(i,j)}.
\]

Now take any element \(x\) appearing in some \(A_i\), and let

\[
n(x)=\min\{n\ge 1:x\in A_n\}.
\]

If \(x\in A_i\), then \(x\in A_{n(x)}\cap A_i=A_{\gcd(n(x),i)}\). By minimality of \(n(x)\), we must have \(\gcd(n(x),i)=n(x)\), so \(n(x)\mid i\). Thus \(x\) belongs to exactly those \(A_i\) whose index is a multiple of \(n(x)\).

Define

\[
B_n=\{x:n(x)=n\}.
\]

Then the \(B_n\) are pairwise disjoint and

\[
A_i=\bigsqcup_{n\mid i}B_n.
\]

Therefore

\[
|A_n|=\sum_{d\mid n}|B_d|.
\]

Since \(|A_d|=d\), Möbius inversion gives

\[
|B_n|=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu\left(\frac nd\right)d=\varphi(n).
\]

So the whole structure is forced: each \(B_n\) has size \(\varphi(n)\), and \(A_i\) is the disjoint union of the \(B_n\) for \(n\mid i\).

---

## 2. A lower bound for the desired sum

Let

\[
D=\{d:d\mid 250\}=\{1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250\}.
\]

For a subset \(S\subseteq D\), let

\[
U(S)=\left|\bigcup_{d\in S}A_d\right|.
\]

Using the decomposition into the disjoint blocks \(B_n\),

\[
U(S)=\sum_{\substack{n\mid d\\ \text{for some }d\in S}}\varphi(n).
\]

Let \(U_k=\min\{U(S):S\subseteq D,\ |S|=k\}\). The minimum values are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
k & \text{a set attaining the minimum} & U_k\\
\hline
1 & \{1\} & 1\\
2 & \{1,2\} & 2\\
3 & \{1,2,5\} & 6\\
4 & \{1,2,5,10\} & 10\\
5 & \{1,2,5,10,25\} & 30\\
6 & \{1,2,5,10,25,50\} & 50\\
7 & \{1,2,5,10,25,50,125\} & 150\\
8 & D & 250
\end{array}
\]

These values are obtained by observing that including \(A_{125}\) or \(A_{250}\) forces the union to have size at least \(125\) or \(250\), so for \(k\le 6\) the minimum must come from \(\{1,2,5,10,25,50\}\), where the table is immediate from the divisibility structure.

Now let

\[
M_{(1)}\le M_{(2)}\le \cdots \le M_{(8)}
\]

be the eight numbers \(\max A_d\) for \(d\mid 250\), written in nondecreasing order. For each \(k\), let \(S_k\subseteq D\) be the set of the \(k\) indices with the smallest maxima. Then every element of \(\bigcup_{d\in S_k}A_d\) is at most \(M_{(k)}\), so

\[
U(S_k)\le M_{(k)}.
\]

But \(U(S_k)\ge U_k\), hence

\[
M_{(k)}\ge U_k.
\]

Therefore

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d
=\sum_{k=1}^8 M_{(k)}
\ge 1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250
=499.
\]

So the desired sum is at least \(499\).

---

## 3. Construction attaining \(499\)

We now construct a valid sequence achieving the bound.

For each \(n\mid 250\), choose disjoint sets \(B_n\) of sizes \(\varphi(n)\) as follows:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
n & \varphi(n) & B_n\\
\hline
1 & 1 & \{1\}\\
2 & 1 & \{2\}\\
5 & 4 & \{3,4,5,6\}\\
10 & 4 & \{7,8,9,10\}\\
25 & 20 & \{11,12,\dots,30\}\\
50 & 20 & \{31,32,\dots,50\}\\
125 & 100 & \{51,52,\dots,150\}\\
250 & 100 & \{151,152,\dots,250\}
\end{array}
\]

For \(n\nmid 250\), choose \(B_n\) to be any set of \(\varphi(n)\) unused positive integers, say all larger than \(250\).

Now define

\[
A_i=\bigcup_{n\mid i}B_n.
\]

Then for any \(i,j\),

\[
A_i\cap A_j=\bigcup_{n\mid i,\ n\mid j}B_n
=\bigcup_{n\mid \gcd(i,j)}B_n,
\]

so

\[
|A_i\cap A_j|
=\sum_{n\mid \gcd(i,j)}\varphi(n)
=\gcd(i,j).
\]

Thus the sequence is valid.

Now compute the maxima for divisors of \(250\):

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1 & 2 & 5 & 10 & 25 & 50 & 125 & 250\\
\hline
\max A_d & 1 & 2 & 6 & 10 & 30 & 50 & 150 & 250
\end{array}
\]

Their sum is

\[
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

Therefore the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]
